intro: A child has her father's chin and her grandmother's laugh. A field of corn stands in rows of plants that are nearly identical. A strain of bacteria in a hospital shrugs off a drug that killed its ancestors ten years ago. All three are the same story told at different speeds. Something inside cells carries instructions, copies them, hands them on, and, once in a while, changes them. This unit is about that something and about what it does over time.

The first chapter goes inside the cell. You will see the shape of DNA, how a cell copies it, how a gene becomes a protein, and how a change of one base can change a life. You will follow Gregor Mendel's peas to learn why traits skip a generation, and follow Queen Victoria's family to see a gene ride down an X chromosome. You will end with the tools that let scientists read a whole genome and edit a single base, and the questions those tools raise.

The second chapter steps back to the whole history of life. The evidence comes from rock layers, from bones, from embryos and from DNA itself, and all of it points the same way. You will meet the fish with a neck, the finches whose beaks changed in one year of drought, and the moths that turned dark with the smoke of factories. By the end you should be able to explain, with evidence, how living things came to be as varied as they are and why they are still changing.
bigQuestion: How do living things pass on their traits, and how does that inheritance, over long stretches of time, produce the variety of life on Earth?

timeline.t: Carl Linnaeus publishes a system for naming and grouping living things in nested categories
Charles Darwin sails on HMS Beagle; he will visit the Galápagos Islands in 1835
Darwin's and Alfred Russel Wallace's papers on natural selection are read together in London
On the Origin of Species is published
Gregor Mendel publishes his pea experiments; almost no one notices for 34 years
Hardy and Weinberg show that allele frequencies stay constant unless something disturbs them
Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling take Photo 51, the X-ray image of DNA
Watson and Crick publish the double-helix model of DNA
Carl Woese names the Archaea; a drought on Daphne Major shifts finch beaks in one year
The Human Genome Project completes its reading of the human DNA sequence
Tiktaalik, the fish with a neck, is found on Ellesmere Island
The first CRISPR gene-editing treatment, for sickle cell disease, is approved in the United States

words.d: the double-helix molecule that stores a cell's instructions in a sequence of four bases
a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one protein
three bases of mRNA that stand for one amino acid or a stop signal
a change in the sequence of bases in DNA
the two-step cell division that makes sex cells with half the usual chromosomes
one version of a gene; each individual carries two for each gene
an allele whose trait shows even when only one copy is present
the process by which individuals with helpful heritable traits leave more offspring, so the traits spread
how many offspring an individual leaves compared with others in its population
body parts in different species that share one plan because of a common ancestor
the splitting of one species into two that can no longer interbreed
an earlier species from which two or more later species descend

test.q: Which base pairs with cytosine in DNA?
test.why: The pairing rule is A with T and G with C.

test.q: The order of steps from gene to protein is:
test.why: A gene is first transcribed into mRNA, then the mRNA is translated into protein.

test.q: Deleting two bases from the middle of a gene will most likely:
choices: Shift the reading frame and change every codon after it
test.why: Two is not a multiple of three, so every codon downstream is read out of frame.

test.q: Which process creates new combinations of alleles in sex cells?
test.why: Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis shuffle alleles into new combinations.

test.q: A cross between two Rr pea plants gives what ratio of round to wrinkled seeds?
test.why: The Punnett square gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr: three round to one wrinkled.

test.q: Red-green color blindness is much more common in men because the allele is:
choices: Recessive and on the X chromosome
test.why: Men have one X, so one recessive allele shows. Women need it on both X chromosomes.

test.q: In a pedigree, two unshaded parents have a shaded child. The trait is:
test.why: Only a recessive allele can be carried unseen by both parents and appear in a child.

test.q: What does CRISPR-Cas9 use to find its target in DNA?
choices: A protein that reads amino acids
A guide RNA matching the target sequence
test.why: The guide RNA pairs with the matching DNA sequence and directs Cas9 to cut there.

test.q: Why did the Tiktaalik team look in rocks about 375 million years old?
choices: Because those rocks are the easiest to reach
Because the transition from fish to land animals should fall between older fish and younger four-legged animals
Because all fossils are that age
Because a local legend described the fossil
test.why: Lobe-finned fish came before 385 million years ago and land animals after 365 million, so the transition should fall between.

test.q: The forelimbs of a human, cat, whale and bat share the same bones. This is evidence of:
test.why: Same plan with different uses is homology, inherited from one ancestor.

test.q: Which statement about natural selection is correct?
choices: Organisms mutate because they need a new trait
Populations change as heritable traits that aid reproduction become more common
test.why: Selection acts on existing heritable variation and shifts the population; individuals do not change their genes.

test.q: After the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, the next generation of finches had:
choices: No beaks that could crack seeds
test.why: Deep-beaked birds survived and bred, and beak depth is heritable.

test.q: Pesticide resistance in insects develops because:
choices: Rare resistant insects survive and reproduce
Insects learn to avoid the spray
Farmers breed resistant insects on purpose
test.why: Spraying selects for resistance alleles already present in a few individuals.

test.q: Two populations of a species are split by a new river for a million years. The most likely result is:
choices: They gather different changes and may become separate species
They merge into one larger species
test.why: Without gene flow, mutation, selection and drift push the two groups apart.

test.q: What redrew the deepest branches of the tree of life in 1977?
choices: Comparing ribosomal RNA, which revealed the Archaea
test.why: Carl Woese's RNA comparisons showed Archaea are a separate domain from Bacteria.

write.prompt: Make a claim: does the evidence support the idea that all living things descend from common ancestors? Use at least three kinds of evidence from this unit (for example fossils, homologous structures, shared broken genes, or the universal genetic code) and explain how each supports or complicates your claim.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Pick three different kinds of evidence, not three fossils. Name a specific example for each, such as Tiktaalik or the GULO gene.
For each piece of evidence, write the reasoning: why would we expect to see this if the claim is true, and not if it is false?
Address the other side: what would count as evidence against your claim, and has it been found?
Use science words from the unit correctly: homologous, common ancestor, transitional form, mutation.
